title: BufferedReader and BufferedWriter
learningObjectives: Read text line by line with BufferedReader and readLine
Write text efficiently with BufferedWriter and newLine
Recognize null as the end-of-input result from readLine
Flush buffered output when an intermediate write must be visible
Close buffered wrappers and their underlying streams safely

understand.concept: BufferedReader.readLine returns null at end of input. BufferedWriter accumulates characters and offers newLine for a platform line separator. Closing a wrapper closes its underlying stream.
understand.whyItMatters: BufferedReader and BufferedWriter helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Why buffering helps

A `BufferedReader` reads characters into an internal buffer so the program can process data without making a low-level read for every character. `BufferedWriter` similarly collects characters before sending them to the underlying writer. Buffering is especially useful for sequential text processing and can reduce the number of expensive I/O operations.

## Read lines safely

`BufferedReader.readLine()` returns a line without its line terminator. It returns `null` when the end of the input is reached. A loop should therefore continue while the returned line is not null. An empty line is an empty string, not null; this distinction matters when preserving blank lines.

## Write lines and flush output

Use `BufferedWriter.write()` to write characters and `newLine()` to write the platform-specific line separator. Call `flush()` when data must be pushed to the underlying writer before it is closed; closing the writer also flushes it. Do not assume every platform uses the same newline characters.

## Resource ownership and testing

Wrap readers and writers in try-with-resources. Closing the outer buffered wrapper closes the underlying resource too. Test empty input, one line, blank lines, a final line without a newline, and a write failure. When exact cross-platform bytes matter, specify the encoding and line-ending policy rather than relying on platform defaults.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var reader = new java.io.BufferedReader(new java.io.StringReader("first\nsecond"))) { System.out.println(reader.readLine()); } } }
examples.explanation: Reads one complete line with BufferedReader.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var writer = new java.io.StringWriter(); var buffered = new java.io.BufferedWriter(writer)) { buffered.write("buffered text"); buffered.flush(); System.out.println(writer); } } }
examples.explanation: Writes buffered characters and flushes them to the underlying writer.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var reader = new java.io.BufferedReader(new java.io.StringReader("a\nb"))) { System.out.println(reader.readLine()); System.out.println(reader.readLine()); System.out.println(reader.readLine()); } } }
examples.explanation: readLine returns null when no more lines remain.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var writer = new java.io.StringWriter(); var buffered = new java.io.BufferedWriter(writer)) { buffered.write("A"); buffered.newLine(); buffered.write("B"); buffered.flush(); System.out.println(writer.toString().replace(System.lineSeparator(), "|")); } } }
examples.explanation: Uses newLine to insert the platform-specific line separator.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var reader = new java.io.BufferedReader(new java.io.StringReader("one"))) { System.out.println(reader.readLine() != null); } } }
examples.explanation: Uses a null check to detect whether a line was read.

practise.guidedTask: Read a multi-line StringReader using BufferedReader.readLine until it returns null. Write a transformed copy with BufferedWriter and newLine.
practise.independentTask: Build a buffered text-file copier that preserves every line and uses try-with-resources for reader and writer.
hints: Use readLine() != null for end-of-file; an empty string represents a blank line.
Use newLine() when platform line separators are intended, and flush when output must be visible before close.
Test empty input, blank lines, a final line without a terminator and cleanup after failure.
practise.challenge: Test empty input, one line without a final newline, several lines and explicit flush/close behavior.
